questions.q: What is the key difference between backpressure and rate limiting?
options: They are two names for exactly the same mechanism
Backpressure reacts to current real-time load, while rate limiting enforces a predetermined cap regardless of current load
Rate limiting only applies to databases, never to APIs
Backpressure can only be implemented in asynchronous systems
questions.explain: Backpressure is a dynamic signal based on actual current conditions, while rate limiting enforces a fixed ceiling set in advance, independent of whether the system is busy right now.

questions.q: What typically happens to a fast producer's work when there is no backpressure mechanism to a slower consumer?
options: The work is automatically discarded safely
The work piles up in an ever-growing queue, which can eventually exhaust memory and degrade or crash the system
The producer automatically slows itself down with no signal needed
The consumer speeds up automatically to match the producer
questions.explain: Without a signal to slow down, excess work accumulates in a queue. An unbounded queue can exhaust memory, leading to severe slowdowns or crashes that affect unrelated requests too.

questions.q: How does the token bucket algorithm differ from leaky bucket?
options: Token bucket allows short bursts up to an accumulated token balance, while leaky bucket enforces a strictly constant processing rate with no bursts
Leaky bucket allows unlimited bursts while token bucket does not
They are identical algorithms with different names
Token bucket can only be used for backpressure, never rate limiting
questions.explain: Token bucket refills at a steady rate and lets accumulated tokens absorb bursts. Leaky bucket processes at a fixed constant rate regardless of arrival pattern, smoothing out any bursts entirely.

Deliberately rejecting or dropping some incoming work to protect the system's ability to serve the rest
A method for encrypting data under heavy load
A type of database replication strategy
questions.explain: Load shedding intentionally sacrifices some requests (ideally lower-priority ones) so the system can continue serving the remaining requests reliably, rather than degrading for everyone.

questions.q: Are Salesforce governor limits (from Lesson 12) an example of backpressure or rate limiting?
options: Backpressure, because they react to the platform's real-time load
Rate limiting, because they apply a predetermined cap per transaction regardless of current platform load
Neither — they are a consensus mechanism
Both equally, with no meaningful distinction
questions.explain: Governor limits enforce the same fixed cap per transaction whether the platform is busy or idle, which matches the definition of rate limiting rather than reactive backpressure.
